title: Latency-first queueing with dynamic priority dropper for Dedicated fleets
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Dedicated fleets occasionally experience tail-latency spikes when best-effort traffic saturates queue depth during bursty ingress. Existing admission layers enforce throughput guards but prioritize throughput fairness, which can cause latency-sensitive customers (e.g., webchat, real-time assistants) to see degraded p95/p99.

Proposal: Implement a latency-first queueing layer and a dynamic priority dropper. The queueing layer maintains per-tenant priority lanes (real-time, interactive, batch) with configurable headroom tokens and soft guarantees. A lightweight admission proxy will: (1) route requests into lanes based on request metadata and SLA tier, (2) allow short-term burst absorption for interactive lanes using reserved burst tokens, and (3) invoke a dynamic priority dropper when total queue depth or token usage exceeds safe headroom.

Dynamic priority dropper behavior: it computes a time-decayed score per request (age, SLA tier, estimated token cost, and historical error budget) and performs probabilistic dropping from lowest-score requests first. The dropper is tunable per-fleet and exposes filters to prefer dropping large token requests or preempt batch lanes before interactive lanes.

Autoscaling integration: the system will emit warm-up triggers when sustained headroom deficit is observed for a configurable window, influencing Dedicated autoscaler to add capacity with priority for fleets with high interactive load. The queueing layer includes metrics that the autoscaler can consume to avoid oscillatory scaling (hysteresis and cooldowns).
acceptance_criteria: Interactive lane p95 latency <= 250ms under mixed load where interactive=30%, batch=50%, best-effort=20% at fleet-utilization up to 80%
When hitting headroom limits, error rate for Gold customers does not exceed 1.5x baseline and degradation is limited to batch/best-effort lanes first
Drop decisions are explainable via per-request drop-cause tags surfaced in logs and Console traces
Autoscaler warm-up triggers reduce tail-latency incidents by >= 40% in the canary region
Feature can be enabled per-customer and toggled via a rollout flag; default off for older Dedicated fleets
infra_changes: small admission proxy sidecar (Go) with eBPF stats export
notes: Trade-offs: probabilistic dropping avoids synchronized bulk evictions but complicates debugging; we mitigate by adding deterministic debug mode and per-request drop_reason tags.
Alternative considered: strict per-tenant token quotas. Rejected because quotas can cause sharp availability cliffs for multi-tenant fleets and make graceful degradation harder.
Rollout plan: (1) unit tests + integration harness, (2) canary region with queues simulated via load generator, (3) opt-in Beta fleets, (4) wide rollout with 48h monitoring guardrails.
Backward compatibility: default behavior preserved unless feature flag enabled; config stored in fleet metadata to allow per-customer tuning.
